title: Ars Live recap: How can we stop publishers from killing their own games?
gist: In an Ars Live interview, Stop Killing Games founder Ross Scott argues that designing online games for end-of-life server handover from the start costs almost nothing because studios already run local test server environments, and reveals the campaign is currently scheduled for inclusion in the EU's Digital Fairness Act after the European Commission deflected its million-signature petition to national courts.

insights.claim: Stop Killing Games founder Ross Scott argues that if a publisher treats end-of-life playability as a design requirement from day one, the cost of enabling a transition to third-party servers is 'extremely low' because it is a design choice rather than an add-on expense.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: If regulators adopt this framing, the compliance cost to games publishers is a forward-looking design mandate on new titles, not a large retroactive writedown on live-service back catalogs.
insights.quote: the cost can be extremely low then because it comes down to developing the game differently rather than having to have all these additional costs
insights.locator: From the technical side, Scott said

insights.claim: Most online-only games already maintain a locally runnable version of their server stack as a test environment so development doesn't stall when a cloud host like Amazon has an outage, meaning the technical foundation for post-shutdown private servers frequently already exists.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Undercuts the industry's main cost objection to preservation mandates and lowers the expected regulatory burden priced into games publishers.
insights.quote: If they already have that, that’s half the battle right there.
insights.locator: Because even online, most online-only games

insights.claim: Ross Scott frames indefinite, undisclosed game shutdown terms as an anomaly that would be illegal in adjacent consumer categories, comparing them to a warranty or insurance policy whose expiry date is simply 'we'll tell you when it expires.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: This analogy is the legal wedge most likely to succeed with regulators; watch for disclosure-of-service-life requirements migrating from games into other digital goods and subscription hardware.
insights.quote: let’s say you got… a warranty for a product, and it doesn’t tell you a year or two; it just tells you, ‘Well, we’ll tell you when it expires.’
insights.locator: Scott noted how the standard practice of shutting down game access

insights.claim: Scott's proposed remedy is disclosure rather than prohibition: publishers who intend to shut a game down after a set period should be required to communicate that horizon at the point of sale.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A disclosure-based remedy is far cheaper for publishers than a mandated server handover, and is the more likely legislative landing zone to underwrite.
insights.locator: Let's say… the plan was to shut down [a game] in five years

themes.theme: EU regulatory path and Commission vs Parliament split

insights.claim: Scott says the European Commission deflected the million-signature petition on game shutdowns by telling member-state courts to handle it individually, which he calls a failure of the Commission's own charter obligation to harmonize policy across member states.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Signals that EU digital-consumer fights will increasingly be routed around the Commission and through Parliament, a slower but more activist channel.
insights.quote: they managed to just dodge it in every way and say, “Oh, yeah, we’ll let the courts in each country handle this, even though our part of our job is to harmonize policy across the member states.”
insights.locator: Instead, they managed to just dodge it

insights.claim: The Commission's refusal to rule on the petition paradoxically strengthened the campaign, because the resulting publicity converted into favorable support inside the EU Parliament.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A regulatory 'loss' that generates attention can be a leading indicator of a later legislative win; don't read a Commission punt as the end of a compliance risk.
insights.locator: But during that time, all the attention from that

insights.claim: As of August 2026 the Stop Killing Games campaign's demands are scheduled to be folded into the EU's Digital Fairness Act, which Scott says coincidentally covers a set of issues the movement fits almost perfectly.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The Digital Fairness Act is the concrete legislative vehicle to track for game-preservation obligations landing on publishers selling into the EU.
insights.quote: we’re scheduled, so far so good, to get included into the Digital Fairness Act

insights.claim: Ross Scott says he considered the state of long-term game access 'intolerable a decade and a half ago' and only started organizing because no more experienced or knowledgeable advocate stepped forward, describing it as drawing the short straw.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The campaign is founder-dependent and lacks institutional backing, which caps its durability but also means the near-term legislative window is unusually personality-driven.
insights.quote: kept hoping someone else would kick this off, [someone] more experienced or knowledgeable, but it felt like nothing was happening
insights.locator: Scott talked with Ars Technica Senior Gaming Editor Kyle Orland
